title: Verify and De-risk Workshop (Lab)
summary: Groups apply a fixed four-step verification routine to a batch of suspect outputs, record an evidence-backed verdict for each, then compare single-source and two-source checking to judge which is more reliable.
objectives: Apply a verification routine to a set of suspect outputs and record the verdict for each.
Compare two verification strategies and judge which is more reliable.

sections.heading: Verify and De-risk Workshop (Lab)
body: One suspect output is easy to check. Ten is where you need a system. Today you run a verification routine on a whole batch, reach an evidence-backed verdict on each, and then judge which checking strategy you would actually trust.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run a verification routine on several suspect outputs and record a clear verdict for each.
I can compare two verification strategies and judge which is more reliable, with a reason.
I can back my verdicts with evidence from a trusted source.

terms.definition: A fixed set of steps applied the same way to every output.
Your conclusion on a claim: verified, false, or unclear.
The trusted-source information that backs your verdict.
Sources that do not copy each other, so they are unlikely to share the same error.
A method you can trust to give the right result repeatedly.

sections.heading: A routine keeps you fair
body: When you check many outputs, it is tempting to judge each one by how confident it sounds. A verification [[routine]] stops that: the same fixed steps apply to every output, so a slick output gets no easy pass.

Our routine has four steps - isolate the claim, pick an independent trusted source, compare, and record a verdict. The [[verdict]] can be verified, false, or unclear, and 'unclear' is an honest answer when the evidence is not there.

sections.heading: Not all checks are equally reliable
body: A single-source check is quick, but if that one source is wrong or out of date, your verdict is wrong too. A two-source cross-check is slower but far harder to fool, because two [[independent sources]] rarely share the same mistake.

Judging which strategy is more [[reliable]] means weighing speed against confidence and asking a sharp question: could these sources fail together? The more independent they are, the more you can trust their agreement.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Work in groups with roles: claim-isolator, source-checker, verdict-recorder, reporter. Run the routine on the whole batch, then compare two strategies on a tricky output.
items: Copy the four routine steps onto your sheet.
For each output, isolate the claim and pick a trusted source.
Compare and record a verdict with its evidence.
Choose one tricky output and check it single-source, then two-source.
Judge which strategy is more reliable and why.
For one false output, write the harm and the check that de-risks it.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which verdict was hardest to reach, and what made it hard?
When is the slower two-source check worth the extra time?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: State which verification strategy you would use and the trade-off you accept.
Note one responsible-use habit this workshop reinforced.

questions.prompt: Apply the four-step routine to each suspect output. Record a verdict and the trusted-source evidence for each.
questions.stem:
The claim is ___
My verdict is ___
Evidence: ___
questions.lookFor: Every verdict must cite the trusted source, not a feeling. Model: 'Verdict: false. The output said the tower was 900 metres; the official source lists a different height, so the claim does not match a trusted source.' Accept 'unclear' as a valid, honest verdict when no source on the reference sheet covers the claim.

questions.prompt: Verify one tricky output single-source, then two-source. Judge which is more reliable and explain using source independence.
questions.stem:
Single-source result: ___
Two-source result: ___
The more reliable strategy is ___ because ___
questions.lookFor: Model: single-source was faster but the one source was out of date; the two-source cross-check caught the error, so it is more reliable. Look for reasoning about source independence and the speed-versus-confidence trade-off, not just which was quicker. Agreement raises confidence but is not proof if the sources could fail together.

questions.prompt: Log every suspect output, your verdict, the evidence, and the strategy used.
questions.stem: Columns: Output | Claim checked | Verdict | Evidence (trusted source) | Strategy used
questions.lookFor: Mastery: a verdict for each output, each backed by cited trusted-source evidence and a named strategy. Partial: verdicts for most outputs but some lack cited evidence. Not yet: verdicts are guesses with no trusted-source evidence.

questions.prompt: Give a verdict on one output with its evidence, and judge which verification strategy is more reliable and why.
questions.lookFor: Applies the routine to reach an evidence-based verdict and judges which verification strategy is more reliable with a reason. Reward evidence-backed verdicts; push students who prefer speed to weigh reliability and source independence.

questions.prompt: Design a three-layer verification for a high-stakes claim about a UAE record, and explain when the extra effort is worth it and when it is not.
questions.lookFor: Stretch target from the pack: designs a three-layer verification for a high-stakes claim and justifies when the extra effort is worth it and when it is not, reasoning about how independent the three sources really are.
